claim: The ability to associate sensory stimuli with abstract classes is critical for survival.
source: The ability to associate sensory stimuli with abstract classes is critical for survival.
evidence: This is a general statement about the importance of sensory-abstract associations for survival, presented as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Experimental studies have probed two kinds of associations between stimuli and categories: fixed associations and flexible ones.
source: Such experiments have probed two kinds of associations between stimuli and categories: fixed associations (Freedman and Assad, 2006; Fitzgerald et al., 2011; Cromer et al., 2010) (in which, e.g., stimuli are either in category A or in category B), and flexible ones (Wallis et al., 2001; Stoet and Snyder, 2004; Roy et al., 2010; Reinert et al., 2021) (in which, e.g., stimuli are in category A in one context and category B in another).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies that have investigated these two types of associations.

claim: Activity of single neurons in associative cortex develops selectivity to task-relevant abstract variables such as category and context.
source: A consistent finding in these experiments is that activity of single neurons in associative cortex develops selectivity to task-relevant abstract variables, such as category (Freedman et al., 2001; Fitzgerald et al., 2011; Reinert et al., 2021) and context (White and Wise, 1999; Wallis et al., 2001; Stoet and Snyder, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple experimental studies showing selectivity development.

claim: Neurons typically display selectivity to multiple abstract variables.
source: Neurons, however, typically display selectivity to multiple abstract variables (Rigotti et al., 2013), and those patterns of mixed selectivity are often hard to intepret (Cromer et al., 2010; Roy et al., 2010; Hirokawa et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies documenting mixed selectivity patterns.

claim: Neurons in visual cortex encode simple sensory variables via negatively correlated responses.
source: Classical work indicates that neurons in visual cortex encode simple sensory variables (e.g., two opposite orientations) via negatively correlated responses (Hubel and Wiesel, 1962; Olshausen and Field, 2004): neurons that respond strongly to a given variable respond weakly to the other one, and vice versa.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to classical studies in visual cortex.

claim: Responses in visual cortex are symmetric, with about the same number of neurons responding strongly to one variable or the other.
source: Those responses, furthermore, are symmetric (DeAngelis and Uka, 2003): about the same number of neurons respond strongly to one variable, or the other.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental work on visual cortex.

claim: Evidence for negatively correlated and symmetric responses has been reported in monkeys and mice prefrontal cortex.
source: Evidence in favour of this type of responses has been reported in monkeys (White and Wise, 1999; Cromer et al., 2010; Roy et al., 2010; Freedman and Miller, 2008) and mice (Reinert et al., 2021) prefrontal cortex (PFC).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies in PFC.

claim: Evidence for positively correlated responses has been reported in experiments from monkeys lateral intraparietal cortex.
source: However, evidence in favour of a different type of responses has been reported in a different set of experiments from monkeys lateral intraparietal (LIP) cortex (Fitzgerald et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental work in LIP cortex.

claim: In LIP cortex, responses to categories A and B were found to be positively correlated.
source: In that case, responses to categories A and B were found to be positively correlated: neurons that learn to respond strongly to category A also respond strongly to category B, and neurons that learn to respond weakly to category A also respond weakly to category B.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental findings cited from Fitzgerald et al., 2013.

claim: In LIP cortex, responses were strongly asymmetric with almost all neurons displaying the strongest response to the same category.
source: Furthermore, responses were strongly asymmetric: almost all neurons displayed the strongest response to the same category (despite monkeys did not display behavioural biases towards one category or the other).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental findings cited from Fitzgerald et al., 2013.

claim: The model hypothesizes that synaptic connectivity in neural circuits evolves by implementing gradient descent on an error function.
source: To this end, we hypothesize that synaptic connectivity in neural circuits evolves by implementing gradient descent on an error function (Richards et al., 2019).
evidence: This is the central hypothesis of the modeling work, with a citation to related work.

claim: Under gradient-descent plasticity, neural networks can achieve high performance on both simple and complex tasks.
source: A large body of work has demonstrated that, under gradient-descent plasticity, neural networks can achieve high performance on both simple and complex tasks (LeCun et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to work on neural network performance.

claim: Gradient-descent learning can be implemented in a biologically plausible way.
source: Recent studies have furthermore shown that gradient-descent learning can be implemented, at least approximately, in a biologically plausible way (Lillicrap et al., 2016; Whittington and Bogacz, 2017; Sacramento et al., 2018; Akrout et al., 2019; Payeur et al., 2021; Pogodin and Latham, 2020; Boopathy and Fiete, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to recent studies on biologically plausible learning.

claim: The model can capture experimental findings showing that neurons become selective to category and context after learning.
source: Via mathematical analysis and simulations, we show that the model can capture the experimental findings discussed above. In particular, after learning, neurons in the model become selective to category and, if present, context; this result is robust, and independent of the details of the circuit and the task.
evidence: This claim is supported by the mathematical analysis and simulations presented in the paper.

claim: Whether correlations after learning are positive or negative depends on circuit and task details.
source: On the other hand, whether correlations after learning are positive or negative, and whether population tuning to different categories is asymmetric or not, is not uniquely determined, but depends on details.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis showing parameter-dependent behavior of correlations.

claim: Activity measures in the model are modulated by circuit details including activation function, learning rates, and initial connectivity.
source: We determined how, in the model, activity measures are modulated by circuit details (activation function of single neurons, learning rates, initial connectivity) and task features (number of stimuli, and whether or not the associations are context dependent).
evidence: This claim is supported by the systematic analysis of parameter dependencies presented in the paper.

claim: The model predicts that selectivity is shaped by connectivity with downstream areas.
source: Second, it predicts that selectivity is shaped by connectivity with downstream areas, a result that is in line with recent experimental observations (Glickfeld et al., 2013; Ye et al., 2016; Hirokawa et al., 2019; Gschwend et al., 2021).
evidence: This prediction is supported by the model analysis and is consistent with cited experimental observations.

claim: For a given neuron, selectivity correlates with the strength of the synaptic connection to downstream neurons that read out category.
source: More specifically, it predicts that, for a given neuron, selectivity correlates with the strength of the synaptic connection that the neuron makes to the downstream neurons that read out category (Figure 5B, C and Figure 8A).
evidence: This prediction is supported by the model analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claim: During learning, some neurons develop mixed selectivity to category and context, others develop pure selectivity to category, but none develop pure selectivity to context.
source: Across all neurons that are strongly connected to downstream readout neurons, selectivity to category and context is distributed in a highly stereotyped way: during learning, some neurons develop mixed selective to category and context, others develop pure selectivity to category, but none develop pure selectivity to context (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the model analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Whether a neuron develops mixed or pure selectivity depends on initial activity.
source: Moreover, whether a neuron develops mixed or pure selectivity depends on initial activity (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Before learning, the category selectivity index is zero on average.
source: Before learning, the responses of single neurons to different stimuli are random and unstructured. Thus, responses to stimuli paired with category A are statistically indistinguishable from responses to stimuli paired with category B (Figure 2A). This makes the category selectivity index zero on average (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: After learning, the category selectivity index for most neurons increases.
source: After learning, the responses of single neurons depend on category: within-category responses become more similar than across-category responses, resulting in two separate distributions (Figure 2E). As a consequence, the category selectivity index for most neuron increases; correspondingly, average selectivity increases from zero to positive values (Figure 2F), thus reproducing the behaviour observed in experimental studies (Freedman et al., 2001; Freedman and Assad, 2006; Reinert et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results (Figure 2E, 2F) and is consistent with cited experimental studies.

claim: The selectivity increase is observed in all circuit models that successfully learned the task, independent of the parameters.
source: We found that the selectivity increase is a universal property – it is observed in all circuit models that successfully learned the task, independent of the parameters.
evidence: This claim is supported by systematic parameter variation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Before learning, activity in response to different stimuli is uncorrelated.
source: As discussed above, before learning the responses of neurons in the intermediate layer are random and unstructured. Thus, activity in response to different stimuli is uncorrelated; this is illustrated in Figure 2C, where all non-diagonal entries of the correlation matrix are close to zero.
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation matrix shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Over learning, the correlation matrices develop structure with correlations becoming different within diagonal and off-diagonal blocks.
source: Over learning, the correlation matrices develop structure. Correlations become different within the two diagonal, and the two off-diagonal blocks, indicating that learning induces category-dependent structure.
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation matrices shown in Figure 2G and 2K.

claim: Varying model details can switch the category correlation from negative to positive.
source: The model does not, however, always produce negative correlation: varying model details – either the parameters of the circuit or the number of stimuli – can switch the category correlation from negative to positive (Fitzgerald et al., 2013; one example is shown in Figure 2K).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results showing parameter-dependent correlation behavior.

claim: Over learning, all activity vectors acquire a component that is aligned with a common, stimulus-independent direction.
source: Over learning, activity vectors in Figure 3A move. Specifically, over learning all activity vectors acquire a component that is aligned with a common, stimulus-independent direction.
evidence: This claim is supported by the mathematical analysis and illustrated in Figure 3.

claim: Category correlation depends on the threshold and gain of the readout neuron.
source: In Figure 4A, we show category correlation as a function of the threshold and gain of the readout neuron (Figure 1C). We find that varying those can change the magnitude and sign of correlations, with positive correlations favoured by large values of the threshold and gain and negative correlations favoured by small values.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Category correlation is affected by the threshold and gain of neurons in the intermediate layer.
source: Category correlation is also affected by the threshold and gain of neurons in the intermediate layer. This can be seen in Figure 4B, which shows that larger values of the threshold and gain tend to favour positive correlation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Category correlation depends on the total number of stimuli.
source: Category correlation also depends on the total number of stimuli, a property of the task rather than the circuit (Materials and methods Simple task: category correlation, Equation 77). This is illustrated in Figure 4D, which shows that increasing the number of stimuli causes a systematic decrease in correlation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 4D and the mathematical derivation.

claim: The model predicts that increasing the number of stimuli should push category correlation from positive to negative values.
source: The model thus makes the experimentally testable prediction that increasing the number of stimuli should push category correlation from positive to negative values.
evidence: This prediction is derived from the analysis of how correlation depends on the number of stimuli.

claim: In the context-dependent task, each trial is specified by both a stimulus and a context cue.
source: On each trial, both a stimulus, and a context cue, are presented to the network.
evidence: This is a description of the task structure used in the model.

claim: Before learning, average category selectivity is weakly negative in the context-dependent task.
source: Before learning, activity is characterized by small selectivity, which is weakly negative on average (Figure 6A; the fact that average category selectivity is initially weakly negative is due to the composite nature of inputs for this task, see Materials and methods Detailed analysis of category selectivity).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 6A and explained by the mathematical analysis.

claim: Over learning, the average category selectivity increases in the context-dependent task.
source: Over learning, the average category selectivity increases (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The average category selectivity increases in all circuit models for the context-dependent task, regardless of the parameters.
source: As in the simple task, we found that the average category selectivity increases in all circuit models, regardless of the parameters (Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by systematic parameter variation analysis.

claim: Average context selectivity increases over learning in the context-dependent task.
source: We find, as we did for category selectivity, that average context selectivity increases over learning – a behaviour that is in agreement with experimental findings (Wallis et al., 2001; Stoet and Snyder, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results and is consistent with cited experimental findings.

claim: The increase in context selectivity is highly robust and does not depend on model details.
source: The increase in context selectivity is, as for category, highly robust, and does not depend on model details (Figure 6H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by systematic parameter variation analysis.

claim: The behavior of correlations in the context-dependent task is variable across circuits.
source: As in the simple task, the matrices acquire additional structure during learning, and that structure can vary significantly across circuits (Figure 6F, I).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results showing different correlation patterns.

claim: Context correlation can either decrease or increase over learning depending on circuit parameters.
source: Context correlation behaves differently in the two circuits displayed in Figure 6F and I: it decreases over learning in Figure 6F, whereas it increases in Figure 6I.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 6F and 6I.

claim: The emergence of context-related structure is a signature of the gradient-descent learning rule.
source: The emergence of context-related structure is, on the other hand, more surprising, since the activity of the readout neuron does not depend on context. Nevertheless, context-dependent structure, in the form of clustering, emerges in the intermediate layer activity. Such novel structure is a signature of the gradient-descent learning rule used by the circuit (Canatar et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis and a citation to related work.

claim: Context clustering emerges because activity changes are determined by both target category and input correlations.
source: But, roughly speaking, context clustering emerges because, for a pair of sensory inputs, how similarly their intermediate-layer representations evolve during learning is determined both by their target category and their correlations (Equation 27, Materials and methods Evolution of connectivity and activity in large circuits).
evidence: This claim is derived from the mathematical analysis of the learning dynamics.

claim: The region of parameter space leading to an increase in correlation shrinks substantially in the context-dependent task compared to the simple task.
source: However, we find that the region of parameter space leading to an increase in correlation shrinks substantially compared to the simple task (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C, see also Materials and methods Context-dependent task: computing activity); this is in line with the observation that correlations decrease to negative values when the complexity of the task increases, as shown in Figure 4D.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C and Figure 4D.

claim: Neurons that strongly increase selectivity to either category or context are, before learning, strongly connected to the downstream readout neuron.
source: As in the simple task, this leads to the prediction that neurons that strongly increase selectivity to either category or context are, before learning, strongly connected to the downstream readout neuron (Figure 8A).
evidence: This prediction is derived from the mathematical analysis and illustrated in Figure 8A.

claim: Among neurons strongly connected to the readout, some increase selectivity to both category and context, others increase selectivity to category but not context, and none increase selectivity to context but not category.
source: We observe that, among all the neurons that strongly increase their selectivity, some increase selectivity to both category and context (orange sample neuron), and others increase selectivity to category, but not context (yellow sample neuron). In contrast, none increases selectivity to context but not category.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The asymmetry between category and context arises because the readout neuron learns to read out category but not context.
source: The asymmetry between category and context arises because, in the model, the readout neuron learns to read out category, but not context.
evidence: This claim is derived from the model structure and analysis.

claim: If a second readout neuron that learns to read out context is included, neurons with strong pure selectivity to context are also observed.
source: We show in Figure 6—figure supplement 3E, F that if a second readout neuron, which learns to read out context, is included in the circuit, neurons with strong pure selectivity to context are also observed.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3E, F.

claim: Pure- and mixed-selective neurons can be distinguished based on patterns of initial response gain.
source: The exact patterns that the response gain takes across the two populations is described in detail in Materials and methods Analysis of patterns of context and category selectivity (Equation 183); the fact that pure- and mixed-selective neurons can be distinguished based on these patterns is illustrated in Figure 8C.
evidence: This claim is supported by the mathematical analysis and illustrated in Figure 8C.

claim: Initial activity plays an important role in learning by breaking symmetry among neurons and determining functional specialization.
source: Overall, these results indicate that initial activity, which is mostly unstructured and task-agnostic, plays an important role in learning: it breaks the symmetry among neurons in the intermediate layer, and determines which functional specialization neurons will display over learning.
evidence: This claim is derived from the analysis of how initial activity patterns determine selectivity outcomes.
